{"id": "dcf9d070-721a-472a-898f-95e304e85be4", "role": "assistant", "content": [{"text": "Here's the honest picture, not just a percentage:

**The catch: not everything in this stack can move to Graviton**

- **RDS for SQL Server — cannot move.** Amazon RDS for SQL Server only supports x86 instance classes (m5, m5d, r5, r5b, r5d, m6i, r6i, m7i, r7i, m8a, r8a, r8i). There is no Graviton/ARM instance class for RDS SQL Server, full stop. This part of the estate gets **zero** savings from this plan — it stays on x86 regardless.
- **40 x m5.xlarge EC2 (Amazon Linux)** — eligible. Amazon Linux 2/2023 has native ARM64 builds, so these can generally move to M6g/M7g/M8g, assuming no x86-only binaries or kernel modules in your AMIs/software.
- **RDS for PostgreSQL 15, db.r5.large** — eligible. PostgreSQL on RDS supports Graviton classes (r6g/r7g/r8g, and newer r9g/m9g are rolling out too), so this can move cleanly.
- **Lambda .zip functions, Python, x86_64** — eligible for arm64, *if* none of your dependencies ship x86-only compiled binaries (some native/C-extension packages need an ARM-built wheel/layer).

**On the CO2 number itself**

AWS's own published figure is that Graviton-based EC2 instances use **up to 60% less energy than comparable x86 instances for the same performance**, with Graviton also delivering up to 40% better price-performance. That's a real, AWS-stated efficiency ratio — but it's not a ready-made "tons of CO2" answer, because actual carbon savings depend on:
- how utilized the 40 instances/DB/Lambda functions actually are today (idle capacity doesn't scale the same way),
- the carbon intensity of the specific AWS region's power grid,
- and real measured energy draw, not just theoretical instance-class efficiency.

I don't have a carbon-footprint calculator in this chat to turn "60% less energy" into an exact kg CO2e figure for your environment — that level of precision comes from AWS's Customer Carbon Footprint Tool, which uses your actual billing/usage history.

**Bottom line:** of your four components, three (the 40 EC2 instances, the PostgreSQL RDS instance, and the Lambda functions) are realistic Graviton migration candidates and would plausibly cut energy use for that portion of the estate by up to ~60% at equivalent performance. The SQL Server RDS instance is locked to x86 and contributes nothing to the savings.

If it'd help, I can look into whether your actual 40 EC2 instances and Lambda functions have any x86-only dependencies that would block the ARM move — that would need to check your account.", "type": "text"}], "created_at": null}
